outlines.version: ISACA AAISM exam content outline (no version shown; page ©2026)

articles.title: Shared Responsibility in Depth: IaaS, PaaS, SaaS and AI
articles.scope: How duties split across IaaS, PaaS, SaaS and AI services, contrasted with shared fate and customer responsibility matrices. The reader can map any service to who owns identity, data, configuration and runtime controls. Builds on the cloud/foundations base term.

articles.title: Cloud Threat Landscape: CSA Top Threats, ATT&CK Cloud Matrices and Breach Patterns
articles.scope: Common cloud threats (misconfiguration, credential theft, management-plane abuse, insecure APIs, supply chain) using CSA Top Threats and the ATT&CK IaaS, SaaS and Identity Provider platforms, with real breach patterns. Contrasts cloud threats with on-premises ones.

articles.title: CSPM vs CWPP vs CNAPP vs CIEM vs DSPM vs KSPM vs AI-SPM
articles.scope: What each posture and protection category detects and misses, plus exposure management, attack paths and agentless scanning. Maps categories to Defender for Cloud and to Security Hub, GuardDuty, Inspector and IAM Access Analyzer; fidelity tables live in cloud/compare.

articles.title: Cloud Workload Security: VMs, Containers, Serverless and PaaS
articles.scope: Hardened golden images, secure and measured boot, workload identity instead of keys, runtime threat detection, configuration baselines and app-platform hardening, contrasted per compute model. Links devops/kubernetes for CKS-depth container security.

articles.title: Isolation in the Cloud: Hypervisors, Multi-Tenancy, Containers and Sandboxes
articles.scope: Management plane vs data plane, type 1 vs type 2 hypervisors, provider isolation designs (AWS Nitro, Azure hypervisor and Azure Boost), container and microVM isolation, and what tenants can and cannot verify.

articles.title: Cloud Vulnerability and Patch Management
articles.scope: Prioritizing with CVSS, EPSS and the KEV catalog; agent vs agentless scanning of VMs, images and functions; patch orchestration and immutable replacement; and SLAs. Contrasts Defender Vulnerability Management and Azure Update Manager with Inspector and Patch Manager.

articles.title: CASB and SaaS Security Posture Management
articles.scope: Shadow IT discovery, API vs proxy CASB modes, session controls, OAuth app governance and SSPM. Shows how CASB differs from SSPM and SWG, and that AWS has no first-party CASB (fidelity none).

articles.title: IoT and OT/ICS Security
articles.scope: Device identity and lifecycle, the Purdue model, IEC 62443 zones and conduits, ATT&CK for ICS, and passive OT monitoring. Contrasts Defender for IoT with AWS IoT Device Defender and IoT policies.

articles.title: Cloud Penetration Testing and Attack Emulation
articles.scope: Provider rules of engagement (AWS penetration testing policy vs Microsoft Cloud Penetration Testing Rules of Engagement), scoping, vulnerability assessment vs pentest vs BAS, and tools such as Pacu, Stratus Red Team, Prowler and ScoutSuite.

articles.title: Using Security Reference Architectures and Capability Maps
articles.scope: How to use capability maps, control benchmarks and multi-account reference designs to draft a target security architecture and roadmap. Links MCRA and MCSB (cloud/azure), AWS SRA (cloud/aws) and their head-to-head (cloud/compare).

articles.title: Guardrails: Preventive, Proactive, Detective and Corrective Controls
articles.scope: Controls that block (SCPs, RCPs, declarative policies, Azure Policy deny and denyAction), evaluate before deployment (Control Tower proactive controls via CloudFormation Hooks), detect (AWS Config, audit) and correct (modify, deployIfNotExists, auto-remediation), plus compensating controls. Bicep, CloudFormation and Terraform examples.

articles.title: Security Baselines for Landing Zones and Multi-Account Estates
articles.scope: Vendor-neutral security topology: log archive and security tooling accounts, delegated administrators, root and break-glass access, tagging strategy and baseline benchmarks (MCSB, FSBP, CIS). Product comparison of Azure landing zones and Control Tower lives in cloud/compare.

articles.title: Multi-Cloud Security Architecture
articles.scope: One security control plane across Azure and AWS: identity federation, centralized posture, unified logging and SIEM, and policy as code. States where native tools stop, and the operating-model trade-offs; links the native-vs-third-party CNAPP ADR in decisions/.

articles.title: Cloud Security Architecture Review Method
articles.scope: A repeatable method to evaluate an existing or proposed design: scoping, control mapping to a benchmark, threat-model linkage, findings, risk acceptance and evidence. The reader can run a review and defend its conclusions.

articles.title: SIEM vs SOAR vs XDR vs EDR vs NDR vs MDR vs ITDR
articles.scope: Separates log correlation, automation, endpoint, network and identity detection, cross-domain XDR, cloud detection and response, UEBA and managed services. Shows how Sentinel with Defender XDR differs from the Security Lake, GuardDuty and Security Hub stack.

articles.title: SOC Operating Model, Triage and Metrics
articles.scope: Tiers vs pods, MDR and MSSP models, incident classification (true, benign and false positive), tuning and suppression, SOC optimization, case management, MTTD and MTTR, and the agentic SOC with human approval.

articles.title: Security Telemetry: Cloud Log Sources and Security Data Lakes
articles.scope: Control-plane, data-plane, identity, M365 and Graph activity, network (VNet flow logs; NSG flow logs retire 2027-09-30; VPC and Transit Gateway flow logs), DNS and workload logs, retention tiers, OCSF vs ASIM, Sentinel data lake vs Security Lake, and CloudTrail Lake with its closed-to-new-customers status.

articles.title: Collecting Security Logs: Agents, Syslog/CEF, WEF and Cloud-Native Pipelines
articles.scope: Azure Monitor Agent with data collection rules, syslog and CEF forwarders, Windows Event Forwarding, policy-driven diagnostic settings and custom tables, versus organization trails, a log archive account and the CloudWatch agent. Includes troubleshooting missing logs and alerts.

articles.title: Detection Engineering and Detection-as-Code
articles.scope: The detection lifecycle (hypothesis, data, logic, test with BAS, tune, retire), coverage mapping against ATT&CK v20 Enterprise, Mobile, ICS and cloud platforms, D3FEND countermeasures, and CI/CD for rules. Compares signature, behavioral and anomaly detections.

articles.title: Writing Detections: Sigma, KQL and Athena SQL
articles.scope: One detection written in Sigma and converted to Sentinel analytics rules (scheduled, NRT), Defender XDR custom detections and Athena SQL over Security Lake. Covers TI, ML and anomaly rules, Fusion's replacement by Defender XDR correlation, and alert tuning. C# and Python test harnesses.

articles.title: KQL, Logs Insights and Athena for Security Hunting
articles.scope: Security tables and query patterns only: advanced hunting tables, KQL jobs and summary rules on the data lake, CloudWatch Logs Insights and Athena over CloudTrail and Security Lake. General KQL syntax is owned by cloud/azure/observability.

articles.title: Threat Hunting in the Cloud
articles.scope: Hypothesis-, intelligence- and anomaly-driven hunting with advanced hunting, Sentinel notebooks connected to the Sentinel MCP server, the Sentinel graph, and Athena over Security Lake. Explains how hunting differs from triage and how findings become detections.

articles.title: Threat Intelligence: IoCs, TTPs, Kill Chains and STIX/TAXII
articles.scope: Intelligence levels, the Pyramid of Pain, kill chain vs ATT&CK, TLP sharing rules and TI platforms. Ingests STIX 2.1/TAXII feeds into Sentinel and GuardDuty threat lists, and uses AI for enrichment with data-source validation.

articles.title: Deception: Honeypots, Honeytokens and Canary Credentials
articles.scope: Decoy systems vs decoy data and credentials, high-fidelity cloud detections such as canary access keys and decoy storage objects, placement, and legal and operational risks.

articles.title: Identity Threat Detection and Response
articles.scope: Token theft, AiTM phishing, password spray, Kerberoasting and pass-the-hash; risk-based detection, session revocation and continuous access evaluation. Contrasts Entra ID Protection and Defender for Identity with GuardDuty IAM findings. Also covers (merged from risk-based-access-and-itdr): Covers access signals (user, device, location, behavior, threat intelligence), user risk vs sign-in risk, and policy outcomes (allow, step-up, block, session limits). Also covers testing policies in report-only mode, workload-identity risk, and identity threat detection and response, with risk-adaptable access control as the CISSP framing. Entra Conditional Access and ID Protection stay in cloud/azure/identity, and the Entra vs AWS pair goes to cloud/compare.

articles.title: EDR Operations: Attack Surface Reduction, Automation Levels and Device Response
articles.scope: Defender for Endpoint advanced features, ASR rules, device groups, automated investigation and automation levels, attack disruption, device timelines, live response and investigation packages, and secure baselines with Intune and Windows LAPS. AWS fidelity: none.

articles.title: Email Threat Protection: Phishing, BEC, Sandboxing and SPF/DKIM/DMARC
articles.scope: Phishing and business email compromise, detonation sandboxing, safe links, sender authentication with SPF, DKIM and DMARC, and investigation and remediation in Defender for Office 365. AWS fidelity: none.

articles.title: Incident Response with NIST SP 800-61r3
articles.scope: The CSF 2.0-aligned model in r3 vs the four-phase lifecycle in r2, roles, severity, communications with stakeholders and regulators, and cloud-specific preparation. The reader can write an IR plan for Azure and AWS.

articles.title: IR Readiness: Pre-Provisioned Access, Game Days and Fault Injection
articles.scope: Pre-provisioned responder roles and forensic accounts, runbook rehearsal, game days, and fault injection with AWS FIS and Resilience Hub vs Azure Chaos Studio. Tabletop exercises stay in practice/tabletops.

articles.title: Investigation and Root-Cause Analysis with Entity Graphs and Timelines
articles.scope: Scoping, timelines, entity pivots, blast radius and root cause. Contrasts the Defender incident graph, attack story and blast radius analysis with Amazon Detective behavior graphs.

articles.title: Containing and Eradicating Cloud Incidents
articles.scope: Per-scenario playbooks for leaked credentials, compromised instances, exposed buckets and tenant takeover: quarantine NSG or security group, deny SCP or RCP, session revocation, key rotation, snapshot isolation and recovery from backups.

articles.title: Cloud Forensics: Evidence Capture on Azure and AWS
articles.scope: Order of volatility, snapshot and memory capture, isolation, chain of custody, ISO/IEC 27037 handling and dedicated forensic accounts, with Python and C# automation. The reader can collect evidence without destroying it.

articles.title: SOAR Playbooks and AI-Assisted Response
articles.scope: Automation rules, playbooks and runbooks; Logic Apps vs EventBridge, Step Functions and Systems Manager. Agentic SecOps with Security Copilot workspaces, roles, plugins and agents, the Sentinel MCP server and the AWS Security Incident Response agent, with approval gates.

articles.title: Network Segmentation vs Microsegmentation
articles.scope: Zones, east-west vs north-south traffic, NSGs and ASGs vs security groups and NACLs, Kubernetes network policies and identity-based segmentation. The reader can pick the right granularity per workload.

articles.title: Firewalls from L3 to L7: Stateless, Stateful, NGFW, IDPS and WAF
articles.scope: What each layer can see and enforce, and TLS inspection trade-offs. Both Azure Firewall Premium and AWS Network Firewall inspect TLS; they differ in rule engine (rule collections vs Suricata), insertion model and central policy.

articles.title: Network Detection, IDS/IPS and Packet Capture in the Cloud
articles.scope: Flow vs packet visibility, IDPS signatures, NDR analytics, and VPC Traffic Mirroring vs Network Watcher packet capture. Notes that SCS-C03 excludes packet-level analysis.

articles.title: Edge Protection: WAF, WAAP, Bot Control and DDoS Resilience
articles.scope: OWASP Top 10 at the edge, managed rules, rate limits, JA3/JA4 fingerprints, geofencing, bot management, API and XML protection, L3/4 vs L7 DDoS and cost protection, across Front Door, Application Gateway, CloudFront and AWS WAF.

articles.title: SASE vs SSE vs ZTNA vs VPN
articles.scope: SWG, CASB, ZTNA, FWaaS and SD-WAN; identity-aware access vs network VPN. Covers Global Secure Access (Entra Internet Access with TLS inspection, threat intelligence, prompt-injection protection, network DLP, shadow-AI discovery and agent controls; Entra Private Access) vs AWS Verified Access and Client VPN. AWS SWG and CASB fidelity: none.

articles.title: Secure Administrative Access: Bastion, JIT and Session Manager vs Jump Hosts
articles.scope: Removing inbound management ports with Azure Bastion, just-in-time access, Session Manager and EC2 Instance Connect; session logging; and why jump hosts fall short. Links security/iam for privileged access workstations.

articles.title: Private Connectivity for PaaS: Private Endpoints, PrivateLink and Data Perimeters
articles.scope: Removing public exposure with private endpoints or PrivateLink, service endpoint policies, Network Security Perimeter (learning vs enforced mode) and AWS data-perimeter policies (RCPs, VPC endpoint policies). Covers DNS pitfalls.

articles.title: Egress Control and Data Exfiltration Prevention
articles.scope: Default-deny egress, FQDN filtering, forced tunneling, NAT and proxy designs, tenant restrictions, and exfiltration detection in flow and DNS logs. Includes egress controls for AI agents.

articles.title: DNS Security: Protective DNS, DNS Firewalls and Tunneling Detection
articles.scope: Resolver logging, filtering, DGA and tunneling detection, DNSSEC limits and private DNS. Compares Azure DNS resolver policy with its Threat Intelligence feed (close for filtering) and Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall Advanced (partial for tunneling detection).

articles.title: Network Exposure and Reachability Analysis
articles.scope: Finding unintended paths with Network Watcher (effective rules, IP flow verify), VNet flow logs, attack paths and Cloud Security Explorer, versus Network Access Analyzer, Reachability Analyzer and Inspector network reachability.

articles.title: Central Network Security Policy at Scale
articles.scope: Organization-wide rules that override local ones: Virtual Network Manager security admin rules and Azure Firewall Manager vs AWS Firewall Manager policies for WAF, security groups, Network Firewall and DNS Firewall. Product comparison lives in cloud/compare.

articles.title: Securing Hybrid and Multicloud Connectivity: IPsec VPN, Private Circuits and MACsec
articles.scope: IPsec site-to-site and point-to-site VPN, ExpressRoute and Direct Connect encryption options including MACsec, Virtual WAN security, and routing hygiene between clouds.

articles.title: Traffic Inspection Architectures: Centralized vs Distributed
articles.scope: Secured hubs in hub-spoke or Virtual WAN vs an inspection VPC behind Transit Gateway and Gateway Load Balancer, symmetric routing, and cost and latency trade-offs. The reader can design inspection that does not break flows.

articles.title: The Cloud Secure Data Lifecycle, Data Flows and Dispersion
articles.scope: The create, store, use, share, archive and destroy phases, controls per phase, data mapping and flows, and dispersion such as erasure coding and bit splitting.

articles.title: Data Discovery, Classification and Labeling
articles.scope: Classification schemes, sensitive info types, EDM, fingerprinting, trainable classifiers, auto-labeling, container and Power BI labels, the information protection client and scanner. Contrasts Purview with Macie data identifiers (partial).

articles.title: Message and Document Encryption: IRM, Purview Message Encryption, S/MIME and TLS
articles.scope: Rights management that travels with content vs transport TLS vs S/MIME, and Purview Message Encryption vs Advanced Message Encryption. AWS fidelity: none.

articles.title: Data Loss Prevention Architectures: Endpoint, Network, Cloud and AI
articles.scope: DLP channels, policy precedence, adaptive protection, false-positive tuning, network DLP and DLP for AI prompts. States that AWS has no first-party DLP enforcement (fidelity none): Macie and CloudWatch Logs data protection only discover or mask.

articles.title: Insider Risk Management and Adaptive Protection
articles.scope: Insider threat models, risk indicators, pseudonymized investigation, risk levels driving DLP, forensic evidence, Activity explorer and alert handling across the Purview portal and Defender XDR.

articles.title: Data Security Posture Management (DSPM), Including for AI
articles.scope: Finding shadow data, oversharing and data exposed to AI. Compares unified Purview DSPM (classic DSPM for AI retires Nov–Dec 2026) and data-aware posture in Defender CSPM with Macie and Security Hub.

articles.title: Securing Object and File Storage
articles.scope: Blocking public access, SAS vs presigned URLs, bucket and container policies, CORS, storage firewalls, and malware scanning with Defender for Storage vs GuardDuty Malware Protection for S3.

articles.title: Database Security: Authentication, Auditing, Activity Monitoring and Threat Protection
articles.scope: Identity-based database auth, auditing, database activity monitoring, dynamic masking and threat protection for Azure SQL, Cosmos DB and Synapse vs RDS Database Activity Streams and GuardDuty RDS Protection.

articles.title: Encryption at Rest: Server-Side, Client-Side and Field-Level
articles.scope: Disk, service, database (TDE, Always Encrypted) and field-level encryption and what each protects against. Compares SSE with CMK, encryption at host and confidential disk encryption with EBS default encryption and NitroTPM, and migrating off Azure Disk Encryption before its 2028-09-15 retirement. Also covers (merged from encryption-placement): Maps the SY0-801 1.3 encryption levels (full disk, partition, file, volume, database, record, transport) to the threat each defeats: a stolen disk, a curious DBA or a compromised app. Weighs key custody and the performance and query trade-offs, and places end-to-end encryption. Data states and classification belong to security/data-protection.

articles.title: Enforcing Encryption in Transit
articles.scope: TLS policies on load balancers and PaaS, mTLS, MACsec on Direct Connect and ExpressRoute Direct, AWS VPC Encryption Controls vs Azure Virtual Network encryption (partial), and enforcement through policy.

articles.title: Data Integrity, Log Integrity and Non-Repudiation
articles.scope: Hashing, signing, versioning and WORM; CloudTrail log file validation vs immutable log storage; code signing; and traceability for audit.

articles.title: Confidential Computing: Encryption in Use
articles.scope: TEEs (SEV-SNP, TDX, Nitro Enclaves), attestation, and confidential VMs, containers and GPUs. States which threats these address and which they do not.

articles.title: Privacy-Enhancing Technologies: Differential Privacy, Clean Rooms, Federated Learning, Homomorphic Encryption
articles.scope: What each PET protects, its cost, and fit for analytics and ML; contrasts AWS Clean Rooms with Azure confidential clean rooms and TEEs with homomorphic encryption. Also covers (merged from privacy-enhancing-cryptography): Explains what each technique lets you compute or prove without revealing inputs, how mature and costly it is, and where it fits: private inference, credential proofs, and MPC or FROST (RFC 9591) threshold key custody. Differential privacy and confidential computing belong to security/data-protection.

articles.title: Tokenization vs Masking vs Format-Preserving Encryption
articles.scope: Vault-based vs vaultless tokenization, static vs dynamic masking, FPE (NIST SP 800-38G) and how each affects PCI scope. C# and Python examples.

articles.title: Ransomware Resilience Strategy and Cyber Recovery
articles.scope: Prioritized resiliency across identity, privileged access, backups and BCDR, isolated recovery environments, and recovery sequencing mapped to the ransomware kill chain. Links architecture/reliability for DR. Also covers (merged from immutable-backups-ransomware-resilience): 3-2-1 and 3-2-1-1-0 rules, WORM and vault locks (governance vs compliance, unlocked vs locked), logically air-gapped vaults, multi-user and multi-party approval, and restore testing. Compares Azure Backup immutable vault with AWS Backup Vault Lock.

articles.title: Data Retention, Legal Hold and Secure Deletion
articles.scope: Retention labels and policies vs storage lifecycle rules, legal hold, eDiscovery, media sanitization (NIST SP 800-88), crypto-shredding and proving deletion in the cloud.

articles.title: Risk Management: Appetite, Assessment and Treatment
articles.scope: Inherent vs residual risk, qualitative vs quantitative methods (FAIR, ALE), ISO 31000 and NIST risk frameworks, risk registers, treatment options and cloud-specific risks.

articles.title: Security Policy Framework: Policies, Standards, Procedures, Guidelines and Exceptions
articles.scope: The policy hierarchy, ownership, exception and risk-acceptance workflow, and keeping policies aligned with cloud and AI change.

articles.title: NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0
articles.scope: The six Functions (including Govern), Profiles and Tiers, and links to SP 800-53, SP 800-61r3 and the preliminary-draft Cyber AI Profile (IR 8596).

articles.title: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 vs SOC 2
articles.scope: Certification vs attestation, ISMS clauses and Annex A vs Trust Services Criteria, Statement of Applicability, Type 1 vs Type 2, and inheriting provider reports.

articles.title: Cloud Audit and Assurance: SOC 1/2/3, SSAE 18 vs ISAE 3402, CUECs and Gap Analysis
articles.scope: Report types and scope restrictions, complementary user entity controls, bridge letters, audit planning, gap analysis, and obtaining reports through AWS Artifact and the Microsoft Service Trust Portal.

articles.title: Product and Cloud Assurance Schemes: Common Criteria, FIPS 140-3, FedRAMP, C5
articles.scope: What each scheme evaluates, how to read a certificate, FIPS 140-3 levels for KMS and HSMs, and the FIPS 140-2 move to the Historical List in September 2026.

articles.title: PCI DSS v4.0.1 in the Cloud
articles.scope: CDE scoping, customized vs defined approach, key v4 requirements (MFA, script integrity, targeted risk analysis), compensating controls and tokenization to shrink scope.

articles.title: GDPR and Privacy Engineering for Cloud Systems
articles.scope: Controller vs processor, lawful basis, DPIAs, data subject rights, pseudonymization, privacy by design and ISO/IEC 27701:2025.

articles.title: Privacy Laws Compared: GDPR, CCPA/CPRA, HIPAA, PIPEDA, LGPD, India DPDP Act
articles.scope: Scope, roles, rights, PII vs PHI, ISO/IEC 27018 and GAPP (now the AICPA Privacy Management Framework), and PIAs, so one privacy program can serve several laws.

articles.title: Cross-Border Transfers, Conflicting Laws and Sovereign Cloud
articles.scope: SCCs, the EU-US Data Privacy Framework, transfer impact assessments, CLOUD Act vs GDPR Art. 48, residency vs sovereignty, the EU Data Boundary and the AWS European Sovereign Cloud.

articles.title: Breach Notification and Incident Reporting Obligations Compared
articles.scope: Triggers, clocks and recipients under GDPR, NIS2, DORA, SEC Form 8-K Item 1.05, HIPAA, the CRA and AI Act Art. 73, plus a regulator communication plan.

articles.title: DORA vs NIS2
articles.scope: Scope, ICT risk management, incident reporting timelines, ICT third-party oversight including ESA-designated critical providers, TLPT and penalties.

articles.title: EU Cyber Resilience Act for Software and Cloud Vendors
articles.scope: Products in scope, essential requirements, SBOM and vulnerability handling, reporting duties applying since 2026-09-11 and full application on 2027-12-11. Links security/supply-chain.

articles.title: Control Frameworks Crosswalk: CSF, ISO 27001/27017, SOC 2, PCI, CIS, CCM, SP 800-53, MCSB
articles.scope: A mapping table for implementing a control once and evidencing it many times, with CIS Controls v8.1 Implementation Groups and CIS Benchmarks.

articles.title: Compliance as Code and Continuous Audit Evidence
articles.scope: Policy as code (Azure Policy, AWS Config, OPA, Checkov), conformance packs, OSCAL, compliance dashboards and evidence automation with Audit Manager and Purview Compliance Manager.

articles.title: Operational Controls: ITIL 4 and ISO/IEC 20000-1 for Secure Cloud Operations
articles.scope: Change, release, configuration, problem, incident, capacity, availability, continuity and service-level management, with COBIT and COSO context. Links devops/sre.

articles.title: Security Metrics, KRIs and Board Reporting
articles.scope: KPIs vs KRIs, risk dashboards, AI security metrics, SEC 10-K Item 1C disclosure and NIS2/DORA management accountability.

articles.title: Cloud Provider and Third-Party Risk: Contracts, Assurance and Exit
articles.scope: Due diligence (CSA STAR, CAIQ, SOC reports), SLA, MSA and SOW terms, right to audit, escrow, cyber insurance, ISO/IEC 27036, lock-in, EU Data Act switching rules and DORA third-party duties.

articles.title: AI Threat Landscape: OWASP LLM Top 10 (2025) and MITRE ATLAS
articles.scope: LLM01–LLM10 with examples (model theft now sits under LLM10 and LLM03), ATLAS tactics and their ATT&CK overlap, and where each risk sits in a RAG or agent architecture.

articles.title: OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications 2026
articles.scope: ASI01–ASI10 with attacks and mitigations, mapped to the LLM Top 10 and ATLAS.

articles.title: Prompt Injection (Direct and Indirect) vs Jailbreaks
articles.scope: Why injection is a trust-boundary flaw, direct and indirect vectors (documents, email, images, tool output) and jailbreaks, with layered defenses: spotlighting, Prompt Shields, the Bedrock prompt-attack filter (user input only) and privilege separation, in C# and Python.

articles.title: Data Poisoning, Model Theft and the AI Supply Chain
articles.scope: Poisoning of training data and RAG sources, backdoors, model serialization attacks, extraction, inversion and membership inference, evasion, AI-BOMs and provenance.

articles.title: Secure AI Reference Architecture
articles.scope: Identity (managed identity, keyless), network isolation, data controls, guardrails, gateway, logging and monitoring for AI apps and agents, aligned to MCSB v2 AI controls and the AWS SRA AI guidance.

articles.title: AI Gateway as a Security Control Point
articles.scope: Token quotas against unbounded consumption, auth, content-safety policies, logging and model routing with the API Management AI gateway for Foundry vs API Gateway and AgentCore Gateway (partial).
articles.boundary: Security-control view only (authentication, policy, content safety and logging enforced at the gateway); the architecture lives in ai-gateway-pattern.

articles.title: Securing RAG and Vector Stores
articles.scope: Permission-aware retrieval, embedding leakage, poisoned sources and tenant isolation; contrasts Azure AI Search document-level access with Bedrock Knowledge Bases metadata filters.

articles.title: Excessive Agency and Least-Agency Agent Authorization
articles.scope: Agent identity, scoped short-lived credentials, tool allowlists, oversight modes, approval flows, sandboxing and kill switches. Links Entra Agent ID and AgentCore Identity and Policy in their owning sections.

articles.title: Securing Multi-Agent Systems: Inter-Agent Trust, Cascading Failures and Rogue Agents
articles.scope: Authenticating and authorizing agent-to-agent calls, message integrity, containing cascading failures and detecting rogue agents (ASI07, ASI08, ASI10). ai/protocols owns A2A itself.

articles.title: Sandboxing Agent Tools and Code Execution
articles.scope: Containing unexpected code execution and local MCP server compromise with containers, gVisor and microVMs; AgentCore Code Interpreter vs Foundry code interpreter. Links appsec/wasm-sandboxing.

articles.title: MCP Security: Tool Poisoning, Confused Deputy, Token Passthrough and More
articles.scope: All eleven sections of the MCP 2026-07-28 Security Best Practices (confused deputy, token passthrough, SSRF, state handle hijacking, local server compromise, authorization URL validation, stdio proxy escalation, mix-up, localhost redirect impersonation, CIMD trust policies, scope minimization) plus community attacks (tool poisoning, rug pulls, shadowing).

articles.title: Data Exfiltration via AI Agents
articles.scope: The lethal trifecta, exfiltration through rendered markdown images and tools, memory poisoning, and controls: egress allowlists, output filtering, network DLP, DLP for AI and provenance.

articles.title: LLM Guardrails Architecture: Content Safety and Foundry Guardrails vs Bedrock Guardrails
articles.scope: Layered guardrails at input, tool call, tool response and output; what classifiers cannot stop; latency and cost. Maps Prompt Shields, task adherence, groundedness (preview), custom categories and blocklists to Bedrock filters, denied topics, PII masking, Automated Reasoning checks and ApplyGuardrail, including image filters.

articles.title: Securing Enterprise AI Assistants and Low-Code Agents
articles.scope: Oversharing remediation, labels and DLP for Microsoft 365 Copilot, Copilot Studio real-time protection, agent management in the Microsoft 365 admin center, and Amazon Q Business access controls.

articles.title: AI Security Posture Management and AI Threat Protection
articles.scope: AI asset discovery, AI-BOM, attack paths and runtime alerts with Defender CSPM AI-SPM and Defender for AI Services and the data and AI security dashboard; the AWS counterpart is partial.

articles.title: Monitoring and Detecting Attacks on AI Systems
articles.scope: Bedrock invocation logging, AgentCore Observability and Foundry tracing as log sources; detections for jailbreaks, tool-call abuse and cost spikes; AI security metrics.

articles.title: AI Red Teaming with PyRIT and garak
articles.scope: Planning and harm taxonomies, automated attack orchestration with PyRIT, garak probe scans and the Foundry AI Red Teaming Agent, scoring and CI regression tests.

articles.title: Human Oversight, Transparency and Content Provenance Controls
articles.scope: Human-in-the-loop vs on-the-loop designs, explanations and disclosures, C2PA content credentials, watermarking and AI Act Art. 50 marking.

articles.title: AI Governance Operating Model: Roles, Committees, Policies and Training
articles.scope: Developer, provider, deployer and user roles, cross-functional committees, acceptable use policy, shadow AI, AI literacy and awareness training, and updating existing policies for AI.

articles.title: AI Governance: NIST AI RMF and GenAI Profile vs ISO/IEC 42001 vs EU AI Act
articles.scope: A voluntary framework vs a certifiable management system vs a law; roles, lifecycle controls, impact assessments (ISO/IEC 42005), OECD principles and a crosswalk to the CSA AICM.

articles.title: EU AI Act for Engineers and Architects
articles.scope: Risk tiers and prohibitions, provider and deployer duties, GPAI and systemic-risk duties, Art. 50 transparency, the AI Omnibus timeline (Annex III to 2027-12-02, Annex I to 2028-08-02) with dated sources, and the technical evidence architects produce.

articles.title: AI Regulation Beyond the EU: South Korea, US Federal and State, China, Japan, UK
articles.scope: The South Korea AI Basic Act, Colorado and other US state laws, federal agency guidance, China's generative AI measures, and the Japanese and UK approaches, compared by scope and duties.

articles.title: How Existing Laws Apply to AI
articles.scope: Privacy, IP and copyright, non-discrimination, consumer protection (FTC unfair or deceptive practices) and product liability (EU Directive 2024/2853) applied to AI systems.

articles.title: Governing the AI Lifecycle: Intake, Impact Assessment, Documentation, Release Gates and Monitoring
articles.scope: Use-case intake, harms matrix and mitigation hierarchy, data provenance and lineage, bias and interpretability testing, model cards, conformity, release gates, drift and post-market monitoring, deactivation.

articles.title: Assessing AI Vendors, Models and Licenses
articles.scope: Data-use and training terms, opt-out policies, open-weight licenses, indemnities, proprietary model risks, and ISO 42001 or CSA STAR for AI evidence.

articles.title: Building an AI Security Program: Inventory, Risk, Controls and AI Incident Response
articles.scope: AI asset inventory and AI-BOMs, risk thresholds, vendor management, AI-specific monitoring, AI incident response and continuity, organized by the AAISM domains.

articles.title: AI Impact Assessments and Documentation: ISO/IEC 42005, DPIA, FRIA, Model and System Cards, Post-Market Monitoring and Decommissioning
articles.scope: Wave 3. Assessments: the ISO/IEC 42005:2025 impact assessment process and its link to ISO/IEC 42001 risk treatment, the DPIA under GDPR Art. 35, the FRIA under EU AI Act Art. 27 for deployers of high-risk systems, and the NIST AI RMF Map function. Artefacts: model cards, system cards, datasheets, Annex IV technical documentation, instructions for use (Art. 13), post-market monitoring plans (Art. 72), serious-incident reporting (Art. 73), and deactivation, localisation and decommissioning policies (AIGP 4.3.7). Provider artefacts: Microsoft transparency notes, AWS AI Service Cards and SageMaker model cards. The article includes a template pack and flags pending changes to AI Act application dates from the EU digital omnibus; check these against the Official Journal.

articles.title: Business Continuity Management and Business Impact Analysis: BIA, BCP vs DRP, ISO 22301 and Exercises
articles.scope: Wave 6. The BCM lifecycle follows ISO 22301:2019 (with its 2024 amendment) and ISO 22313. The BIA covers MTPD/MTD, RTO, RPO, MBCO, prioritised activities and external dependencies, including cloud providers and SaaS. It then covers continuity strategies and how BCP, DRP, incident response plans and crisis management plans relate, plus crisis communications. Exercise types run from checklist and tabletop through simulation and parallel to full interruption, followed by maintenance and review. NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 and the DORA ICT continuity requirements are cross-referenced. It hands off to architecture/reliability/rto-rpo-dr-strategies and compare/resilience-migration/backup-and-disaster-recovery-azure-vs-aws for the technical side.

articles.title: Security Assessment and Testing Programme: Vulnerability Assessment, Penetration Test, Red and Purple Teams, BAS, Control Testing and SOC 2 Reports
articles.scope: Wave 6. Strategy: internal, external and third-party assessments and audits, and where they run (on-premises, cloud, hybrid). Test types are contrasted: vulnerability assessment, penetration test, red team and purple team, and breach and attack simulation. Engagements: rules of engagement and cloud provider testing policies. Methods: NIST SP 800-115, PTES and TIBER-EU/DORA TLPT. Control testing: design vs operating effectiveness, and SOC 2 Type I vs Type II (with SOC 1, SOC 3 and ISAE 3402). Other testing: synthetic transactions, code review, misuse-case testing, coverage analysis, and security process data such as KPIs and KRIs. Results: reporting, remediation, exception handling and ethical disclosure. It links to cloud-penetration-testing, ai-red-teaming and iso-27001-vs-soc-2.

articles.title: Personnel Security, Security Awareness and Professional Ethics
articles.scope: Wave 6. Ethics: the ISC2 Code of Ethics canons and organisational codes. Personnel controls: screening and hiring, employment agreements (NDA, acceptable use), onboarding, transfers and termination, and vendor, consultant and contractor controls. Administrative controls: separation of duties, job rotation, mandatory vacation and least privilege. Awareness: awareness vs training vs education, phishing simulation, social engineering, security champions and gamification, measuring programme effectiveness, and periodic content reviews for AI, deepfakes and cryptocurrency fraud. It also covers application-security training for developers (CCSP 4.1).

articles.title: Investigations, Evidence Handling and Legal Hold
articles.scope: Wave 6. Investigation types: administrative, criminal, civil, regulatory and industry-standard, each with its standard of proof. Evidence: types and admissibility, ISO/IEC 27037, 27041, 27042 and 27043, chain of custody, order of volatility (RFC 3227), forensic images and hashing, and artefact sources (data, host, network, mobile). eDiscovery and the EDRM model. Legal hold in Purview eDiscovery, S3 Object Lock legal hold and AWS Backup Vault Lock. Cloud issues: jurisdiction, and communication with vendors, customers, partners and regulators (CCSP 5.5). It complements detection-response/cloud-forensics, which covers acquisition technique.

articles.title: Network Protocols and Secure Components: OSI and TCP/IP, Secure Protocols, NAC, Wireless, Cellular, VoIP and CDN
articles.scope: Wave 4. Models: OSI vs TCP/IP layers and the attacks at each layer, and IPv4 vs IPv6 addressing modes. Secure protocol choices: TLS 1.3, IPsec, SSH, DNSSEC and DoH, and SFTP vs FTPS. Converged protocols: iSCSI and VoIP (SIP, SRTP). Network access control: 802.1X with EAP-TLS, and pre- vs post-admission checks. Wireless: WPA3-Personal (SAE) vs WPA3-Enterprise, Bluetooth and Zigbee risks. Cellular: 4G vs 5G security (SUPI concealment, slicing). It also covers transmission media, CDNs as security components, SDN and SD-WAN, and performance metrics. It is the CISSP-level foundation under cloud-networking-fundamentals.

articles.title: Endpoint and Mobile Device Security: UEM and MDM, Baselines, App Control, Windows LAPS and BYOD
articles.scope: Wave 4. Management models: UEM/MDM vs MAM, and enrolment models (corporate, COPE, BYOD). Configuration: security baselines (CIS, Microsoft security baselines, STIGs) and application control (App Control for Business, AppLocker, macOS notarisation). Privilege: Windows LAPS with Entra ID or AD backup and rotation, removing local admin rights and endpoint privilege management. Protection: disk encryption, patch and update rings, mobile threat defence, and EDR as a layer (linked). Scope extends to server requirements across operating systems (SC-100 3.2.1) and a brief look at IoT and OT. Vendor-neutral, with Intune and Defender pointers to cloud/azure/security-services/intune-and-defender-for-endpoint-orientation and AWS Systems Manager pointers for servers.

terms.definition: The 3-2-1 rule plus one immutable or offline copy and zero errors in restore tests.
Redirecting an agent's objectives, usually through injected content, so it pursues the attacker's goal.
Risks from third-party agents, tools, MCP servers, prompts and plugins loaded at runtime.
Rules for which AI tools employees may use, with what data and for what purposes.
An AI incident causing death, serious harm, critical infrastructure disruption or rights infringement that must be reported to authorities.
An inventory of an AI system's models, datasets and dependencies with their provenance, extending the SBOM idea.
Under the EU AI Act, a party using an AI system under its authority in a professional context.
Runtime controls that inspect and filter model inputs, outputs and agent tool calls for safety, security and policy violations.
An assessment of an AI system's likely effects on individuals, groups and society, guided by ISO/IEC 42005:2025.
The EU AI Act duty for providers and deployers to ensure sufficient AI competence among staff, applying since 2 February 2025.
Under the EU AI Act, the party that develops an AI system or model and places it on the market under its name.
Adversarial testing of AI systems for security and safety failures, combining manual probing with automated attack tools.
Discovery of AI models, agents, data and services with assessment of their misconfigurations, exposures and attack paths.
A backup copy isolated, physically or logically, so a compromised source environment cannot reach it.
Expected yearly loss from a risk, calculated as single loss expectancy times annualized rate of occurrence.
Irreversibly transforming data so no individual can be identified by reasonably likely means, taking it outside GDPR.
Detecting and controlling automated traffic using signatures, fingerprints, challenges and behavior.
Automated, safe emulation of attacker techniques to validate that controls and detections work.
Signed provenance metadata, defined by C2PA, recording how media was created and edited, including by AI.
A broker between users and cloud services that discovers shadow IT and enforces access, data and threat policies through API or proxy modes.
One agent's error or compromise propagating through connected agents and systems.
A documented, tamper-evident record of who collected, handled and transferred evidence, which keeps it admissible.
A prioritized set of 18 control groups with safeguards sorted into Implementation Groups; v8.1 added a Govern function.
An OAuth client registration method used by MCP in which the client ID is an HTTPS URL to the client's metadata, bringing SSRF and impersonation risks.
The application encrypts data before sending it, so the service never sees plaintext.
A US law letting US authorities compel US providers to disclose data they control regardless of storage location.

terms.definition: Runtime threat detection and response that correlates control-plane, identity and workload activity in cloud environments.
The create, store, use, share, archive and destroy phases used to place data controls.
A platform combining CSPM, CWPP, CIEM, DSPM and code-to-cloud scanning that shares context such as attack paths.
A US state law requiring developers and deployers of high-risk AI to prevent algorithmic discrimination; its effective date has been delayed.
A key-value event format carried over syslog, widely used by security appliances.
Controls a SOC report assumes the customer operates; without them the provider's controls may not achieve their objectives.
Expressing compliance requirements as machine-evaluated policies and tests so controls are checked and evidenced continuously.
Protecting data while it is processed, inside hardware-based trusted execution environments whose integrity is attested.
A whole virtual machine running in a hardware TEE with memory encryption and attested disk-key release.
The pre-market process showing a high-risk AI system meets AI Act requirements, by internal control or a notified body.
A recurring program that scopes, discovers, prioritizes and validates exploitable exposures, then drives their remediation.
A control that restores a compliant state after detection, such as automated remediation or an Azure Policy modify effect.
A provider designated under DORA by the European Supervisory Authorities and placed under direct EU oversight.
CSA's vendor-agnostic framework of AI control objectives, mapped to ISO/IEC 42001 and the EU AI Act.
CSA's cloud-specific control framework, mapped to major standards and paired with the CAIQ questionnaire.
CSA's public registry of providers' self-assessments, certifications and attestations.

terms.definition: The Cloud Security Alliance's periodic ranking of the most significant cloud security threats, with case studies.
Tooling that continuously checks cloud control-plane configuration against benchmarks and policies to find misconfigurations.
A per-service table stating whether the provider, the customer or both implement and evidence each control.
A standard for scoring the technical severity of vulnerabilities, currently v4.0.
Protection for running VMs, containers and serverless functions through vulnerability scanning, hardening and runtime threat detection.
A seven-stage linear model of an intrusion, from reconnaissance to actions on objectives.
The EU regulation on products with digital elements; its reporting duties apply from 11 September 2026 and full application from 11 December 2027.
Analyzed information about adversaries' capabilities, infrastructure and intent at strategic, operational and tactical levels.
Assigning sensitivity categories to data so handling, protection and retention controls apply consistently.
The party that decides the purposes and means of processing personal data.
Unauthorized transfer of data out of an environment through the network, storage sharing, APIs or AI agents.
Obscuring values, permanently in a copy (static) or at query time for unauthorized viewers (dynamic).
Manipulating training, fine-tuning, embedding or retrieval data to plant bias, backdoors or other misbehavior in a model.
A party that processes personal data on a controller's behalf and under its instructions.
The recorded origin, ownership and transformation history of training and retrieval data.
Independent monitoring of database queries and privileged activity to detect misuse.
Absorbing and filtering volumetric, protocol and application-layer floods so services stay available.
Keeping detection rules in version control with code review, automated tests and CI/CD deployment.
Designing, building, testing, deploying and maintaining threat detections as managed, measurable artifacts.
A control that identifies non-compliant state or activity after it occurs, such as an AWS Config rule or an Azure Policy audit effect.
Adding calibrated noise to results so the presence of any one individual has a provably bounded effect.
Prompt injection typed into the conversation by the user.
Policies and tooling that detect and stop sensitive data leaving approved locations or being shared inappropriately.
Recording each DNS query and response at the resolver, a key source for detecting C2, DGA and tunneling.
Hiding data or C2 traffic inside DNS queries and responses to bypass network controls.
A malware technique that generates many pseudo-random domains so C2 survives blocklisting.
The EU regulation, applying since 17 January 2025, setting ICT risk, incident reporting, resilience testing and ICT third-party rules for financial entities.
An assessment GDPR requires for high-risk processing, identifying risks to individuals and mitigating measures.
Discovering where sensitive data lives, who can access it and how it is exposed, including to AI apps and agents.
Traffic between workloads inside an environment.
Identifying, preserving, collecting and producing electronically stored information for legal matters.
Agent-based endpoint telemetry and detection with response actions such as device isolation and live response.
Allowing outbound traffic only to approved destinations, by FQDN, IP or service, to prevent exfiltration and C2.
Encrypting stored data so access to media, snapshots or the storage layer does not expose plaintext.
Protecting data as it moves between systems, typically with TLS, IPsec or MACsec.
A daily-updated probability that a vulnerability will be exploited in the next 30 days, used to prioritize patching.
The EU's risk-based AI law with prohibitions, high-risk obligations, GPAI duties and transparency rules, phased in over several years.
The EU regulation, applying since 12 September 2025, that includes cloud-switching, portability and switching-charge rules.
Crafted inputs that cause a model to misclassify at inference time.
Classification that matches content against hashed copies of real sensitive values instead of generic patterns.
Giving an LLM application more functions, permissions or autonomy than it needs, so a manipulated model can take harmful actions.
Outside-in discovery and monitoring of internet-facing assets, including unknown or forgotten ones.
A quantitative model expressing risk as the probable frequency and magnitude of future loss.
The US federal program for authorizing cloud services against NIST SP 800-53 baselines.
Records of L3/L4 connections (addresses, ports, protocol, action, bytes) captured at the network layer without payloads.
Reversible encryption whose ciphertext keeps the plaintext's format and length, such as a 16-digit card number.
An assessment certain deployers of high-risk AI must perform on effects for people's fundamental rights before use.
NVIDIA's open-source LLM vulnerability scanner that runs probe and detector suites for injection, leakage and toxicity.
The EU regulation on processing personal data, covering lawful bases, rights, breach notification and international transfers.
Under the EU AI Act, a model able to perform a wide range of tasks; since 2 August 2025 its provider owes documentation, copyright-policy and training-data summary duties.
A hardened, versioned base image from which instances or containers are built, rebuilt rather than patched in place.
A GPAI model with high-impact capabilities, presumed above 10^25 training FLOP, whose provider must also evaluate, red-team, report serious incidents and ensure cybersecurity.
The combined practice of setting security direction, managing risk and demonstrating that obligations are met.
Checking whether model output is supported by supplied source material, flagging ungrounded claims.

Under AI Act Art. 6, an AI system that is a product, or a safety component of one, under Annex I legislation requiring third-party conformity assessment, or one used in an Annex III area unless the Art. 6(3) exception applies.
The US law, amended by HITECH, setting privacy, security and breach rules for PHI held by covered entities and business associates.
A decoy system that attracts attackers so their activity can be detected and studied.
A decoy credential, record or file whose use signals an intrusion with very few false positives.
Abusing users' trust in an agent to win approval for harmful actions or disclosures.
Software that runs virtual machines, either on bare metal (type 1) or on a host operating system (type 2).
Exploiting an agent's inherited or delegated credentials and permissions to act beyond the user's intent.
Systems that detect (IDS) or block (IPS) malicious traffic using signatures and anomaly detection.
A series of standards for securing industrial automation and control systems using zones, conduits and security levels.
Passing model output unvalidated to downstream interpreters, enabling XSS, SQL injection or command execution.
Labeling a closed alert or incident as true positive, benign positive or false positive to drive tuning and metrics.
An observable artifact, such as a file hash, IP address, domain or URL, that signals a likely intrusion.
Injected instructions hidden in content the model processes, such as documents, emails, web pages, images or tool output.
Encryption-based protection attached to content that controls what users can do with it wherever it goes.
Unauthenticated, unencrypted or unvalidated messages between agents that allow spoofing or tampering.
International guidelines for enterprise risk management principles, framework and process; not certifiable.
The certifiable standard for a service management system.
The certifiable standard for an information security management system, with 93 Annex A controls.
Guidance on information security controls specific to cloud services, for providers and customers.
A code of practice for protecting PII in public clouds acting as PII processors.
The certifiable standard for a privacy information management system, standalone since its 2025 edition.
The certifiable standard for an AI management system (AIMS), structured like ISO/IEC 27001.
A separate, trusted environment where systems are restored and validated before returning to production after an attack.
A framework of IT service management practices such as change, incident, problem and service-level management.
A technique that gets around a model's safety training or usage policy to produce disallowed output.
A leading metric that signals rising risk exposure, unlike a KPI that measures performance.
CISA's list of vulnerabilities with confirmed in-the-wild exploitation, widely used to set patch deadlines.
Continuous assessment of Kubernetes cluster and workload configuration against benchmarks such as the CIS Kubernetes Benchmark.
Pivoting from an initial foothold to other systems or identities to reach the attacker's objective.
Least privilege applied to autonomy: minimum tools, permissions and independence, with approval for high-impact actions.
Suspending deletion of relevant data, regardless of retention settings, while litigation or investigation is pending.
An agent with private data access, exposure to untrusted content and an external communication channel, which together enable exfiltration.
False or misleading model output, including hallucinations, that users or systems rely on.
Risks from third-party models, adapters, datasets and libraries used to build LLM applications.
The provider APIs and consoles that create and configure resources; its compromise affects everything behind it.
An MCP server changing a tool's definition or behavior after the user approved it.
An outsourced, round-the-clock service that monitors, investigates and responds to threats on the customer's behalf.
Making data on storage media unrecoverable by clearing, purging or destroying it.
Inferring whether a specific record was in a model's training data from the model's outputs.
Planting malicious content in an agent's persistent memory or context so it influences later sessions.
Fine-grained, per-workload policy, often based on identity or labels, that controls east-west traffic.
MITRE's ATT&CK-style knowledge base of adversary tactics, techniques and case studies against AI systems, including agents.
aliases: Adversarial Threat Landscape for Artificial-Intelligence Systems

terms.definition: An OAuth attack in which a malicious authorization server obtains a code issued by an honest one; mitigated by validating iss.
Obtaining a model's weights or functionality by theft or systematic querying; OWASP 2025 covers it under LLM10 and LLM03.
Reconstructing sensitive training data or attributes from a model's outputs.
Code execution hidden in model files that run code when loaded, such as Python pickle formats.
Requiring a second, independent party to approve destructive or security-weakening operations.
Detection of threats and lateral movement from network traffic and flow metadata, with response actions.
Dividing a network into zones and controlling traffic between them to limit lateral movement and blast radius.
A firewall adding application awareness, IDPS, URL filtering and TLS inspection to stateful filtering.
The EU directive placing cybersecurity risk-management and incident-reporting duties on essential and important entities, transposed by each member state.
NIST's 2024 AI RMF profile describing 12 risks that generative AI creates or worsens, with suggested actions.
NIST's voluntary AI risk management framework with four functions: Govern, Map, Measure and Manage.
NIST's 2024 outcome-based framework of six Functions (Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover), used through Profiles and Tiers.
A preliminary-draft CSF 2.0 Community Profile for securing AI systems, using AI for defense and thwarting AI-enabled attacks.
NIST's catalog of security and privacy controls, the basis of FedRAMP baselines.
NIST's April 2025 incident response guidance, published as a CSF 2.0 Community Profile, superseding the four-phase lifecycle of r2.
Traffic crossing the environment's perimeter, to or from the internet or on-premises networks.
An open, vendor-neutral schema for security events, used natively by Amazon Security Lake and the current AWS Security Hub (Security Hub CSPM still uses ASFF).
Intergovernmental principles for trustworthy AI and recommendations for policymakers, updated in 2024.
The rule to capture evidence from most to least volatile, such as memory before disk.
NIST's machine-readable formats for control catalogs, system security plans and assessment results.
OWASP's December 2025 list of top agentic AI risks, from ASI01 Agent Goal Hijack to ASI10 Rogue Agents.
The OWASP GenAI Security Project's 2025 list of the most critical LLM application risks, LLM01 to LLM10.
The payment card industry standard for protecting cardholder data; v4.0.1 is current and its future-dated requirements became mandatory on 31 March 2025.
Individually identifiable health information protected under HIPAA.
Information that identifies or can be linked to an individual.
A provider's systematic collection and review of performance and incident data after an AI system is released.
A control that blocks a non-compliant action at request time, such as an SCP or an Azure Policy deny effect.
A general assessment of a system's privacy risks, required by some laws and used beyond GDPR.
A control that evaluates a resource definition before deployment, such as a Control Tower proactive control implemented with CloudFormation Hooks.
AI uses banned outright under the EU AI Act, such as social scoring and manipulative techniques.
Crafted input that makes an LLM follow an attacker's instructions instead of the developer's, possible because instructions and data share one channel.
A resolver service that refuses to resolve malicious or disallowed domains and logs every query.
Replacing identifiers so data cannot be linked to a person without separately held information; under GDPR it remains personal data.
A layered reference model for segmenting industrial control networks from enterprise IT.
A model ranking indicator types by how costly each is for an attacker to change, from hashes at the bottom to TTPs at the top.
Microsoft's open-source framework for orchestrating and scoring automated, multi-turn attacks on generative AI systems.
Attacks that encrypt or steal data for extortion, often targeting backups and identity systems first.
A contract clause allowing a customer or regulator to audit a provider, often satisfied by third-party reports.
The amount and type of risk an organization is willing to pursue or retain to meet its objectives.
Choosing to avoid, mitigate, transfer, share or accept a risk.
An agent acting outside its intended scope, through compromise or misalignment, while appearing legitimate.
A cloud-delivered architecture combining SD-WAN networking with Security Service Edge functions.
US rules requiring public companies to disclose material incidents within four business days and describe cyber risk governance annually.
A proxy that filters user web traffic by category, reputation and content, often with TLS inspection.
Low-cost, long-retention storage of normalized security telemetry queried by multiple analytics tools.
An automated organization-wide control that prevents or detects deviation from security policy without reviewing each change.
A predefined response procedure for one incident type, such as phishing or an exposed key, often partly automated.
An LLM application revealing personal, proprietary or credential data through its outputs.
The service encrypts data as it writes it and decrypts on authorized read, with provider- or customer-managed keys.
Use of unsanctioned AI apps, models or agents, often with sensitive data.
A model in which the provider actively shares in customer security outcomes through secure defaults, blueprints and guidance, beyond the contractual split of duties.
A platform that collects, normalizes, stores and correlates security logs to detect, investigate and report on threats.
A detection written in Sigma, a vendor-neutral YAML format that converts to backend queries such as KQL or SQL.
Technology that orchestrates and automates response workflows across security tools using playbooks.
An attestation report on a service organization's controls relevant to customers' financial reporting.
An AICPA attestation on controls against the Trust Services Criteria; Type 1 covers design at a point in time, Type 2 operating effectiveness over a period.
South Korea's framework AI law with duties for high-impact and generative AI, reported effective from 22 January 2026.
aliases: Framework Act on AI Development and Establishment of Trust

terms.definition: Marking untrusted content by delimiting, datamarking or encoding so the model treats it as data, not instructions.
The US attestation standard under which SOC reports are issued; ISAE 3402 is the international counterpart.
The security part of SASE: secure web gateway, CASB, ZTNA and firewall as a service, delivered from the cloud.
Continuous assessment of SaaS tenant settings, sharing and OAuth app grants against security baselines.
European Commission-approved contract terms that legitimize personal-data transfers to countries without adequacy.
Using a stolen or guessed state handle minted by a stateless MCP server to access another user's state.
A firewall that tracks connection state so return traffic is allowed automatically, unlike a stateless ACL.
OASIS standards for expressing threat intelligence (STIX) and exchanging it over HTTPS (TAXII).
The standard protocol and message format for sending Linux and appliance logs to a collector.
Exposure of system prompt contents, which is harmful when they contain secrets or security logic that should not live there.
Assessing and monitoring risks from suppliers, including cloud and AI providers, across the relationship lifecycle.
Proactively searching, usually from a hypothesis, for threats that have evaded existing detections.
Intelligence-driven red teaming of live production systems required under DORA for significant financial entities.
Decrypting, inspecting and re-encrypting TLS traffic at a proxy or firewall, with privacy, pinning and trust-store trade-offs.
An agent using legitimate tools in unsafe or unintended ways, often after manipulation.
Hiding malicious instructions in an MCP or agent tool's description or metadata, which the model reads but the user does not see.
A malicious tool whose description alters how the model uses tools from other, trusted servers.
Copying packets from network interfaces to IDS or forensic tools for deep inspection.
Learning normal behavior of users and entities so that anomalies indicating compromise or insider risk stand out.
Uncontrolled inference use causing denial of service, runaway cost or model extraction through the API.
An agent generating or triggering code that runs with real privileges outside intended bounds.
RAG risks such as cross-tenant retrieval, embedding inversion and poisoned vector stores.
WAF, API protection, bot management and DDoS mitigation combined into one edge service.
An HTTP-layer filter using managed and custom rules to block web attacks such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting.
Detection and response that natively correlates telemetry from endpoints, identities, email, cloud apps and workloads into unified incidents.
Per-application access granted after verifying identity and context, without placing the user on the network.

pairs.difference: CSPM checks control-plane configuration through APIs; CWPP protects what runs inside workloads (vulnerabilities, malware, runtime behavior).
A CASB governs how users and apps access and move data in SaaS; SSPM checks how the SaaS tenant itself is configured.
DSPM finds where sensitive data sits and how exposed it is; DLP enforces policy as data moves or is shared.
A SIEM ingests and correlates any log source you bring; XDR deeply correlates its own vendor's telemetry and takes response actions out of the box.
A SIEM adds analytics rules, incidents and workflows on hot data; a security data lake is cheap long-term storage that other tools query.
IoCs are cheap for attackers to change (hashes, IPs); TTPs describe behavior, so detections built on them last longer.
The kill chain is a linear seven-stage model; ATT&CK is a non-linear matrix of tactics and hundreds of techniques used for detection coverage.
Sigma is a portable rule format that must be compiled to a backend; KQL is an executable query language tied to Microsoft data platforms.
Detection engineering builds tested rules that run continuously; hunting is human-led, hypothesis-driven searching whose findings feed new detections.
A playbook defines the response strategy and decisions for an incident type; a runbook gives exact steps for one task, often automated.
A honeypot is a decoy system that must be built and maintained; a honeytoken is a decoy credential or record whose mere use is an alert.
r2 used a four-phase incident lifecycle; r3 recasts incident response as a CSF 2.0 Community Profile across all six Functions, including Govern.
A preventive control blocks the API request at run time (SCP, Policy deny); a proactive control rejects the resource definition before deployment (CloudFormation Hook).
A preventive guardrail stops the change from happening; a detective guardrail reports the violation after it happens.
CVSS rates how severe a vulnerability is if exploited; EPSS estimates how likely it is to be exploited soon, so the two together drive prioritization.
Segmentation controls traffic between zones or subnets; microsegmentation enforces policy per workload, often by identity or label rather than IP.
A stateful firewall filters on L3/L4 connection state; a WAF parses HTTP and blocks application-layer attacks such as injection.
SSE is only the cloud-delivered security stack (SWG, CASB, ZTNA, FWaaS); SASE adds SD-WAN networking to it.
A VPN places the user on a network segment; ZTNA brokers access to one application at a time after verifying identity and device context.
Protective DNS blocks resolution of malicious domains; DNSSEC only proves records were not tampered with and blocks nothing.
Encryption at rest protects stored bytes, but data is decrypted in memory for processing; confidential computing keeps it protected in memory inside an attested TEE.
With server-side encryption the service sees plaintext and holds or uses the key; with client-side encryption only the application ever sees plaintext.

A vault-based token has no mathematical link to the value, so systems holding only tokens can leave PCI scope; FPE ciphertext is reversible by anyone with the key, so key access keeps systems in scope.
Pseudonymized data can be re-identified with separately held information and remains personal data; anonymized data cannot and falls outside GDPR.
Crypto-shredding destroys keys so ciphertext anywhere becomes useless; media sanitization clears or destroys the physical media, which cloud customers cannot do themselves.
Immutability stops modification or deletion of copies; air-gapping stops a compromised source environment from reaching the copies at all.
3-2-1 assumes off-site copies are safe; 3-2-1-1-0 adds an immutable or offline copy and verified restores because ransomware targets backups.
ISO 27001 certifies a management system against a standard; SOC 2 is an auditor's opinion on controls against the Trust Services Criteria, with Type 2 testing operation over a period.
SOC 1 covers controls relevant to customers' financial reporting; SOC 2 covers security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality and privacy.
The controller decides why and how personal data is processed and carries primary accountability; the processor acts only on the controller's instructions.
Residency is where data physically sits; sovereignty is whose laws can reach it, which can include a foreign provider's home jurisdiction regardless of location.
DORA is a directly applicable regulation for the financial sector with direct oversight of critical ICT providers; NIS2 is a cross-sector directive that each member state transposes.
Inherent risk is measured before controls; residual risk remains after controls and is what gets compared with risk appetite.
CSF is a voluntary outcome framework with no certification; ISO 27001 is a certifiable management-system standard with mandatory clauses.
CIS Controls are a prioritized security program framework; CIS Benchmarks are configuration settings for specific products.
A DPIA under GDPR covers risks from processing personal data; a FRIA under the AI Act covers a high-risk AI system's effects on all fundamental rights, even without personal data.
In direct injection the user is the attacker; in indirect injection the attacker plants instructions in content the system ingests, hijacking an innocent user's session.
A jailbreak defeats the model's safety policy to get forbidden output; prompt injection overrides the application's instructions to hijack its behavior or tools.
Extraction steals the model (weights or behavior); inversion recovers the training data or sensitive attributes behind it.
The LLM list covers risks in model-centric apps; the agentic list covers autonomy risks such as goal hijack, tool misuse, inter-agent communication, cascading failures and rogue agents.
ATT&CK catalogs attacks on enterprise IT; ATLAS catalogs attacks on AI systems and reuses ATT&CK tactics where they overlap.
Tool poisoning hides malicious instructions in a tool definition from the start; a rug pull swaps an approved, benign definition for a malicious one later.
A confused deputy misuses its own authority for a caller; token passthrough forwards the caller's token unvalidated, which breaks audience binding and can create a confused deputy downstream.
In the loop, nothing happens until a human approves; on the loop, the AI acts and a human monitors and can intervene.
The AI RMF is voluntary risk guidance with no audit; ISO 42001 defines a management system that can be certified.
Alignment is safety trained into the model's weights; guardrails are external runtime classifiers and policies that can be tuned, logged and updated without retraining.

Facts verified on 2026-10-24 by fetching primary pages (WebSearch budget was exhausted, so no searches were run):
- ATT&CK v20.0 has been current since 2026-10-13. The Enterprise matrix has 15 tactics. TA0005 is now "Stealth" and TA0112 "Defense Impairment" is new; TA0112 was created 2026-04-14, which places the split in v19.
- The MCRA Learn page links the April 2025 version (page updated 2026-02-04). The draft's "June 2026" claim was removed.
- The Learn page is titled "Overview of DNS resolver policy" (2026-08-11). It covers allow/block/alert rules, domain lists and an MSRC-sourced Threat Intelligence feed.
- Global Secure Access is the unifying term for Entra Internet Access and Entra Private Access. Internet Access lists TLS inspection, threat intelligence, prompt injection protection, DLP, shadow AI discovery and network controls for agents (requires an Agent 365 license).
- The Bedrock prompt-attack filter covers user input only. It requires input tags with InvokeModel, and it does not evaluate tool results or tool definitions. Prompt leakage detection is Standard tier only.
- AWS Network Firewall TLS inspection supports inbound, outbound or both.
- Azure Disk Encryption retires 2028-09-15. After that date, ADE disks fail to unlock on reboot; migrate to encryption at host.
- CloudTrail Lake has been closed to new customers since 2026-05-31; existing customers are unaffected.
- On Defender portal onboarding, Fusion is disabled and Defender XDR correlation replaces it. Custom detections are recommended for detections spanning Sentinel and XDR tables, and alert tuning now applies to Sentinel alerts.
- The MCP 2026-07-28 Security Best Practices has 11 sections, all now in mcp-security. Session hijacking guidance applies only to 2025-11-25 and earlier.
- From the Commission's AI Act page:
  - The AI Omnibus entered into force on 27 July 2026, linked as OJ L 2026/1744.
  - Annex III high-risk obligations move to 2 December 2027 and Annex I to 2 August 2028.
  - Transparency rules apply from August 2026.
  - A ninth prohibition (non-consensual sexual content and CSAM) applies from December 2026.
  - Dates were kept out of the glossary definitions.
- NIST IR 8596 is still an initial preliminary draft (2025-12-16).
- The OWASP Agentic Top 10 was dated 2025-12-09. Its item titles come from memory and secondary sources; check them against the PDF.
